In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the government's policy is not only morally unjustifiable but is also socially damaging.
the current government's policies are unjust because they are based on an erroneous view of the contribution that lone parents make to the social good.

(1) the government's argument that lone parents are ‘non-participatory’ in the labour market is false; (2) lone parents are ‘participating’ in the labour of reproduction and social stability; (3) this participation deserves more recognition in terms of social security benefits and other policy initiatives; (4) this recognition is a matter of justice and fairness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lone parents are not ‘non-participants’ in society, but are ‘participants’ in the unpaid reproductive labour of society.
the UK government's social construction of lone parents as ‘welfare dependent’, ‘non-participatory’ and ‘unproductive’ has been highly influential in justifying cuts to their benefits.
the government's policies are based on a desert argument, but one that has been socially constructed in a manner that is not only unjust but also self-defeating.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to reclaim desert arguments as a basis for a more inclusive and just society, rather than to concede them to the right.
desert arguments have a role to play in justifying social security benefits to lone parents, but that they need to be developed and defended more fully than has been the case in the UK.
the desert ground in debates about lone parent social security is still open and that there is much to be done to reclaim it.
